strengths: Significance: Reducing the number of SAE latents needed for concept suppression is a useful practical objective. Prompt-derived supervision offers an inexpensive way to improve controllability without modifying the diffusion model’s weights.

Empirical promise: Table 1 reports an average UA/IRA/CRA of 91.51 versus 82.29 for SAeUron, with improvements in all three metrics. Sequential removal also shows substantial gains: 92.4% versus 64% UA for nine objects, with better retention.

Originality: Supervised concept assignment within diffusion-model SAEs is a plausible incremental contribution over unsupervised feature selection. The comparisons of supervision objectives, training from scratch versus fine-tuning, and steering strengths provide useful empirical exploration.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and intervention mechanism are generally understandable. The appendix usefully reports four-seed variability, concept-specific failures, and the weaker single-latent nudity result rather than concealing these limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The method does not establish the claimed one-to-one mappings or elimination of feature splitting. Independently choosing each concept’s highest-scoring latent does not ensure distinct assignments. Equation (8) rewards activation on positive examples but neither directly penalizes activation on negative examples nor prevents other latents from encoding the same concept. Table 8 reports ten Cats–Dogs overlap timesteps for the selected model, exactly matching SAeUron. These findings support improved steering, but not the categorical centralization claims.

Soundness—objective: Equation (9) minimizes signed Pearson correlation. This favors negative correlation rather than zero correlation, and positive and negative terms can cancel. Consequently, the stated interpretation as a decorrelation constraint is not justified by the written objective. The implemented loss needs clarification and an appropriate ablation.

Evidence for centralization: A larger score peak and similar k-NN accuracy using selected versus all features establish predictive usefulness, not exclusive localization. The paper should test how much concept information remains after excluding the assigned latent and measure selectivity across concepts. Figure 5 also lacks essential protocol details, including k, data splits, spatial aggregation, and how concept-specific single-feature selection produces the reported classification task.

Evaluation reliability: Section 4.2 says SAeUron’s public metric computation was corrected without describing the error or correction sufficiently to audit the comparison. Tables 1 and 5 give different UA/IRA/CRA values for the designated main model while reporting the same average, 91.51; Table 5’s components actually average to 91.17. These discrepancies need reconciliation, including consistent evaluation and tuning procedures across baselines.

Reproducibility: Important details are missing or delegated too broadly to prior work: SAE dimensions and TopK setting, optimizer, learning rate, training duration, activation sampling, and train/validation/test separation. Assignment also depends on timestep in Equation (4), whereas the mapping is written without timestep dependence; collision handling and assignment updates are unspecified. These omissions materially hinder reproduction.

Efficiency and scope: The 96.67% reduction counts seven versus 210 evaluations in chosen search grids, rather than measured total computational savings. It excludes supervised training and model-selection costs. Sequential scalability is evaluated on one ordered set of nine objects, and architectural generality is asserted without experiments beyond SD v1.x. The practical benefits are promising, but broader claims need narrower wording or additional evidence.

Safety evidence and interpretation: Post-attack UA is only 28.30%, despite outperforming SAeUron, and the different pre-attack accuracy from Table 1 is insufficiently explained. For nudity, the single-latent method yields 47 detections versus SAeUron’s 18; the two-latent variant achieves nine but also changes steering strength from -49 to -60, confounding the comparison. Detector-only evaluation supports a limited suppression claim, not reliable prevention. No material ethical violation is evident, but deployment-oriented safety claims should reflect these limitations.

strengths: Significance: Reducing the number of SAE features needed for concept suppression is a useful practical objective. Table 1 reports an encouraging improvement over SAeUron from 82.29 to 91.51 in average unlearning/retention accuracy, with improvements in all three constituent metrics.

Originality: Supervising selected SAE latents using object and style labels derived from generation prompts is a meaningful extension of unsupervised SAE steering. It provides a concrete mechanism for strengthening concept associations without changing the underlying diffusion model weights.

Evaluation: The paper includes loss variants, training from scratch versus fine-tuning, multiplier sweeps, sequential removal, adversarial prompting, and nudity suppression. Reporting four-seed variability and unsuccessful variants is valuable.

Presentation and limitations: The main pipeline is understandable and supported by qualitative examples. The appendix candidly reports difficult concepts, sensitivity to the supervision coefficient, and the failure of single-latent nudity suppression to outperform SAeUron.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The objective does not establish the claimed one-to-one mapping or elimination of feature splitting. Equation (8) rewards activation on positive examples but does not explicitly penalize activation on negatives or concept information in other latents. Independently selecting each concept's highest-scoring latent does not ensure unique assignments, and no collision-resolution procedure is specified. Indeed, Table 8 reports 10 timesteps with overlapping top latents for Cats and Dogs in the principal OS-DC-CA-FT model, equal to the baseline. Stronger association is plausible; exclusive localization is not demonstrated.

Soundness—decorrelation objective: Equation (9) minimizes signed Pearson correlation, whose minimum encourages anticorrelation rather than zero correlation. Correlations of opposite signs can also cancel in the average. Consequently, the stated loss does not implement the claimed decorrelation penalty. This matters because the decorrelation variant is the main reported model.

Mechanistic evidence: A larger score peak and comparable classification accuracy from selected latents versus all latents show that selected features are informative, not that other features contain no concept information. Figure 5 lacks a probe on the remaining representation after removing the selected features, and the k-NN protocol is insufficiently specified. Causal interventions and residual-information tests are needed to substantiate the paper's principal interpretability claim.

Evaluation consistency: Table 5 identifies OS-DC-CA-FT as the main method but reports UA/IRA/CRA of 91.75/93.16/88.60, whereas Tables 1–2 report 94.65/91.39/88.48. Both give an average of 91.51, although the Table 5 values average to approximately 91.17. The correction to SAeUron's evaluation is also not described sufficiently to audit its effect or establish consistent treatment of other baselines. These unresolved discrepancies weaken confidence in the headline comparison.

Reproducibility: The manuscript omits essential training details such as the optimizer, learning rate, training duration, concrete SAE sparsity settings, and batch size. It does not clearly specify whether concept assignments are fixed across timesteps, how hyperparameters are selected on held-out data, or how decoded interventions are inserted into the diffusion computation. Referring to SAeUron's setup does not fully specify the new supervised procedure or corrected evaluation.

Significance and efficiency: The 96.67% figure is a reduction in a particular search grid from 210 to 7 evaluations, not a measured reduction in total computation. Additional supervised training, method-level tuning, and inference overhead are unquantified. The nine-object sequential experiment is promising but uses one selected sequence, with retention reaching only 60.9%; it does not establish broad scalability or minimal collateral damage.

Limitations and safety claims: Under adversarial attack, unlearning accuracy falls from 73.30% to 28.30%, leaving substantial vulnerability despite improvement over SAeUron. For nudity, the single-latent method produces 47 detections versus SAeUron's 18; the improved result of 9 requires two latents and a different multiplier. This supports a useful suppression mechanism but qualifies the general single-neuron claim. No material ethical violation is evident, but the deployment discussion should distinguish reversible inference-time suppression from durable removal of knowledge and acknowledge detector-based evaluation limits.

strengths: Originality: Supervising diffusion-model SAE latents using prompt-derived concept labels is a useful extension of SAeUron. The approach offers a practical way to strengthen concept-specific steering without changing the base model weights.

Significance: The reported UnlearnCanvas results are promising: Table 1 improves average UA/IRA/CRA from 82.29% to 91.51%. Sequential removal of nine objects also improves UA from 64% to 92.4%, with better retention.

Evaluation: The manuscript includes loss variants, multiplier sweeps, four-seed summary statistics, adversarial evaluation, and an additional nudity-removal experiment. These provide useful evidence beyond isolated qualitative examples.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline and motivation are understandable. The appendix candidly reports difficult object categories, failure with excessive supervision strength, and weaker single-neuron nudity removal.

A dominant score peak and similar top-feature/all-feature k-NN accuracy demonstrate predictive usefulness, not exclusive information localization. Probing the remaining latents after removing the assigned feature and reporting assignment collisions would directly test the claim. Table 8 actually reports ten Cats–Dogs overlapping timesteps for the main variant, matching the baseline.

Soundness—loss formulation: Eq. (9) minimizes signed Pearson correlation. This rewards negative correlation rather than independence, and positive and negative correlations can cancel. Consequently, the stated decorrelation interpretation is unsupported as written. The implemented objective needs clarification and comparison with an absolute or squared correlation penalty.

Evaluation reliability: Section 4.2 says SAeUron metrics were corrected but does not describe the error, correction, or implications for comparability with other baselines. There are also unresolved reporting discrepancies: Table 5 identifies the main variant but lists different UA/IRA/CRA values from Table 1, and its listed components average to approximately 91.17%, not the reported 91.51%. Reproducibility: Essential supervised-training details are absent, including optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training duration, and explicit SAE width and TopK settings. The manuscript also leaves unclear the training/validation/test separation, multiplier-selection objective, handling of latent-assignment collisions and timestep dependence, and k-NN protocol. Referring to the baseline setup does not fully specify the new supervised procedure.

Significance and efficiency: The 96.67% saving counts a chosen search grid shrinking from 210 to seven evaluations; it is not an end-to-end computational measurement and excludes supervised training and its additional tuning. Experiments use SD v1.x and predominantly structured, predefined object/style concepts. This supports a specialized contribution, but broader architecture-transfer and general concept-centralization claims remain untested.

Robustness and safety interpretation: Under attack, UA falls from 73.30% to 28.30%; Figure 9 also shows several other methods with higher post-attack UA. The result supports improvement over SAeUron, not broad adversarial robustness. Nudity removal improves over SAeUron only with the two-latent variant; the single-latent method produces 47 detections versus 18. These are useful, honestly reported limitations, but the conclusions should distinguish reversible inference-time suppression from removal of the underlying capability and avoid implying reliable safety guarantees. No separate material research-ethics violation is evident.

strengths: Significance: Supervised concept-aligned SAE steering addresses a useful practical problem: reducing the effort needed to identify intervention features while preserving unrelated generation. Table 1 reports substantial improvements over SAeUron across object unlearning, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention, increasing their average from 82.29% to 91.51%.

Originality: Combining prompt-derived supervision with sparse activation steering is a meaningful extension of existing SAE-based erasure. The contribution is primarily improved representation organization and controllability rather than a fundamentally new erasure mechanism.

Evaluation: The experiments cover object and style erasure, sequential removal, two adversarial attacks, nudity suppression, held-out styles, and several training variants. Appendix A.4 reports variability across four seeds, and the ablations help establish the value of object/style supervision.

Presentation and ethics: The overall pipeline is understandable and supported by useful qualitative examples. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges reversibility, vocabulary constraints, interference, and architectural limitations. Its impact statement appropriately discusses misuse and incomplete suppression; there is no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The evidence does not establish that feature splitting is eliminated or that concept information resides exclusively in one neuron. Larger score peaks and comparable top-feature versus all-feature classification establish predictive usefulness, not absence of information elsewhere. A complementary test should measure recoverability from the remaining latents after excluding the assigned neuron. Moreover, Table 11 reports that the main model still has ten timesteps where Cats and Dogs share the most active latent, identical to SAeUron. These findings support improved steering features, but not the repeatedly asserted one-to-one encoding.

Soundness—objective and assignment: Equation (8) only rewards assigned neurons on positive examples; it neither directly suppresses their activation on negative examples nor prevents other neurons from encoding the same concept. Independently choosing each concept's highest-scoring neuron also does not ensure an injective assignment, and collision handling is unspecified. Equation (9) minimizes signed Pearson correlation, which rewards negative correlation rather than minimizing dependence. The claimed decorrelation mechanism therefore differs from the stated objective.

Results consistency: Appendix A.10 identifies OS-DC-CA-FT as the main model, but Table 8 gives UA/IRA/CRA of 91.75/93.16/88.60, whereas Tables 1 and 5 give 94.65/91.39/88.48. Table 8 also reports a 91.51 average although its entries average to 91.17. The manuscript does not explain different settings behind these discrepancies, preventing confident interpretation of the headline result.

Reproducibility: Important procedural details remain unspecified, including total training duration, exact training/validation separation when both use the anchor prompts, assignment handling across timesteps, and the criterion used to select erasure multipliers. The central k-NN experiment lacks its neighborhood size, data split, feature aggregation, and a clear explanation of how concept-specific single features produce the reported 20-class accuracy. Appendix A.2 selects loss weights by comparing validation values of objectives whose weights themselves change, without explaining why these values are comparable.

Efficiency: The 96.67% reduction is the arithmetic reduction from a particular 210-setting inference search to seven settings, rather than a demonstrated reduction in total computational cost. The supervised method additionally searches 27 training configurations and reports approximately 5.4 times the per-step training cost in Table 3. End-to-end timing or an amortization analysis is needed to substantiate the broader efficiency claims.

Scope of supporting evidence: The strongest nudity result uses two neurons and a multiplier of -600, while the single-neuron configuration produces 47 detections versus SAeUron's 18 (Table 13). This is a useful practical variant, but weakens the general single-neuron erasure narrative. Likewise, white-box attacked UA is only 57.50%, held-out-style UA is 53.07%, and SDXL-Turbo retention is 45.15%. These results demonstrate relative improvements in some settings, but do not substantiate broad claims of robust, transferable concept centralization. The useful empirical contribution is outweighed by unresolved methodological claims and reporting inconsistencies.

strengths: Significance: Supervised concept alignment is a useful direction for making SAE-based diffusion interventions easier to control. Table 1 reports substantial improvements over SAeUron: average object performance rises from 82.29% to 91.51%, with gains in both erasure and retention.

Originality: Combining prompt-derived supervision with sparse latent steering provides a meaningful incremental contribution over unsupervised SAE-based erasure. The practical benefit of steering fewer latents is valuable even without establishing exclusive concept localization.

Evaluation: The experiments cover object and style erasure, sequential removal, two adversarial attacks, nudity suppression, and several training variants. Appendix A.4 reports four-seed variability, and the appendix includes useful negative results and interference analyses.

Presentation and ethics: The main pipeline is understandable, and the limitations explicitly acknowledge vocabulary constraints, architectural transfer, and concept interference. The impact statement appropriately discusses misuse and false confidence in incomplete erasure; no material ethical violation is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The objective does not establish the claimed one-to-one mappings or elimination of feature splitting. Equation (8) rewards assigned latents on positive examples but does not explicitly suppress their responses on negative examples or prevent other latents from encoding the same concept. Selecting each concept's highest-scoring latent also does not ensure an injective assignment. Table 11 reports 10 Cats–Dogs overlapping timesteps for the main model, matching the baseline. These issues undermine the central mechanistic interpretation, although they do not negate the reported benchmark gains.

Soundness—decorrelation objective: Equation (9) minimizes signed Pearson correlation. Its minimum favors anticorrelation rather than zero correlation, so strongly dependent, anticorrelated features can be rewarded. This differs materially from the stated disentanglement objective. The paper needs to clarify the implemented loss and establish whether its conclusions survive an appropriate dependence penalty.

Evidence for localization: Larger score peaks and comparable top-feature versus all-feature k-NN accuracy demonstrate predictive information in selected latents, not its absence elsewhere. Figure 5 lacks the decisive comparison against all remaining latents after excluding the assigned features. Residual-information probes and controlled ablations are needed before claiming that concept information is confined to one neuron.

Presentation and numerical reliability: The main model's results disagree across tables. Table 1 reports UA/IRA/CRA of 94.65/91.39/88.48, whereas Table 8 reports 91.75/93.16/88.60 for the explicitly identified main variant. Both list an average of 91.51, although the latter values average to 91.17. Reconciling these results is necessary to assess the headline improvement and ablations.

Reproducibility: Important details remain unspecified, including the final training duration, collision handling and timestep dependence of concept assignments, and the k-NN configuration and data split. Section 4.1 states that anchor prompts are also used for validation without clearly explaining sample independence. Selecting different loss weights by comparing their differently weighted validation objectives also needs justification or a common selection metric.

Efficiency: The 96.67% reduction accurately describes the selected 210-versus-7 intervention search grids, but it does not establish an equivalent reduction in overall computational cost. Appendix A.2 introduces a 27-configuration training search, and Table 3 reports approximately 5.4 times the training-step cost. An end-to-end or amortized cost comparison is needed to support the broader efficiency language.

Scope and robustness: Some conclusions exceed the evidence. White-box attack UA falls from 97.60% to 57.50%, indicating substantial remaining vulnerability despite improvement over SAeUron. For nudity, the one-latent model is worse than SAeUron (47 versus 18 detections); the nine-detection result changes both latent count and multiplier, from −49 to −600, confounding their effects. Sequential object evaluation uses one selected sequence, and held-out generalization is demonstrated only for styles. These are promising results, but they do not yet support the breadth of the central claims.

strengths: Significance: Supervised SAE steering addresses a useful practical problem: reducing the number of latent interventions needed for selective concept suppression. Table 1 reports a substantial improvement over SAeUron, from 82.29% to 91.51% average object-unlearning performance, with gains in both erasure and retention.

Originality: Adding prompt-derived supervision to diffusion-model SAEs is a meaningful extension of prior unsupervised steering methods. The combination of concept assignment and object–style separation offers a plausible route to more controllable representations.

Evaluation: The manuscript examines object and style erasure, sequential interventions, two adversarial attacks, nudity suppression, and held-out styles. Appendix A.4 reports results across four seeds, and the exploratory variants provide useful evidence about alternative training objectives.

Presentation and ethics: The overall pipeline is understandable and supported by qualitative examples. The limitations appropriately acknowledge vocabulary constraints, interference, and architectural transfer. The impact statement recognizes misuse and incomplete suppression, and the paper explicitly discloses that removing the SAE restores the original model.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The method does not establish the claimed one-to-one mappings or elimination of feature splitting. Independently assigning each concept its highest-scoring latent does not ensure distinct assignments. Equation (8) encourages activation on positive examples without explicitly suppressing activation on negative examples or removing concept information from other latents. Consistent with this concern, Table 11 reports ten Cats–Dogs overlapping timesteps for the chosen model, unchanged from SAeUron. Larger score peaks and comparable top-latent versus all-latent classification accuracy demonstrate useful predictive features, but not exclusive information localization. A probe on the remaining latents and systematic causal ablations are needed.

Soundness—objective: Equation (9) minimizes signed Pearson correlations. This rewards negative correlation rather than independence, and positive and negative correlations can cancel. Consequently, the stated decorrelation objective does not mathematically enforce the advertised separation. The authors should clarify whether the implementation uses this expression or an absolute/squared correlation penalty and evaluate the distinction.

Results consistency: Table 1 reports UA/IRA/CRA of 94.65/91.39/88.48, whereas Table 8 reports 91.75/93.16/88.60 for the configuration explicitly identified as the main method. Both have the same average, but imply different erasure–retention tradeoffs. The manuscript does not reconcile these results. Similarly, Appendix A.15 claims matching or improving every style metric although IRA and CRA decrease. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the precise comparative claims.

Reproducibility: Important experimental details remain unspecified, including the total training schedule, assignment collision handling and timestep dependence, the k-NN sampling/splitting protocol, and the exact held-out style partition. Section 4.1 states that training anchor prompts are also used for validation without explaining how activations are separated. Appendix A.2 selects loss weights by comparing the weighted validation objective across different weights, which changes the criterion being compared. These choices require clarification and a fixed validation criterion.

Efficiency: The 96.67% reduction is valid for the specified 210-versus-7 evaluation grids, but does not establish an equivalent reduction in total computational cost. Table 3 reports approximately 5.4 times higher training time per measured unit, and the proposed method additionally searches 27 training configurations. Reporting end-to-end costs and the number of erasure requests needed to amortize training would substantiate the practical efficiency claim.

Scope of evidence: Several broader conclusions exceed the results. Sequential object erasure uses one chosen sequence and retains only 60.9% RA after nine removals. Held-out-style UA is 53.07%, and SDXL-Turbo IRA falls to 45.15%. The best nudity result requires two latents and a multiplier of −600; the single-latent version has 47 detections versus SAeUron’s 18. These candidly reported results are valuable, but support a narrower claim of improved supervised steering rather than generally reliable single-neuron erasure. Overall, the empirical promise does not yet outweigh the unresolved methodological and evidential weaknesses.
